It does not stand so much as **rest**, distributing weight across a wide footprint the way a tripod does, except it has six or eight limbs and uses only a few at a time while the others brace.

Bones are not delicate lattices. They are dense columns with almost no marrow cavity, wrapped in tendons like cables. Muscle is not bulky in the showy sense; it is short-fibered and arranged for continuous load, the way a climber’s forearms stay hard even at rest. Skin is thick, leathery, and often armored with mineralized knobs, because a fall from even a small height is an impact, not a stumble.

### How it moves
It does not leap. A jump that would be trivial on Earth would slam it back down hard enough to crack ordinary bone. Instead it **flows**: a slow, deliberate shuffle, one foot planted before the last leaves the ground. When it must go faster, it drops even lower and scuttles, belly nearly brushing the surface, using friction more than stride length.

Claws or hoof-pads are broad and slightly cupped, gripping stone and packed soil. On loose ground it sinks; evolution favors habitats of bedrock, packed clay, and shallow basins where the body can sprawl without vanishing into dust.

### Circulation and breath
Blood in this gravity wants to pool in the lowest tissues and abandon the brain. The plinthwalker solves that by having almost no “up.” Its heart is not one pump but a chain of thick muscular chambers spaced along the body, each pushing blood only a short distance. Vessels are heavily muscled, and valves are numerous. Resting blood pressure, by Earth standards, would be extreme; for it, that is simply what it takes to keep the brain—tucked low in the dome, not perched on a neck—perfused.

Vision is tuned for motion at ground level and for the sheen of water or mineral crust, not for scanning a distant horizon. Hearing is conducted through the feet and belly plates; the ground is a better telegraph than thin air when everything is heavy.

Food is whatever can be reached without rearing: mats of low vegetation, mineral-rich crusts, slow burrowers it can pin with its body. Its silhouette is a flattened oval, more tortoise than mammal, with no neck worth the name. The head is a reinforced wedge set between the shoulders, eyes small and set in bony pits so a fall or a rockslide cannot gouge them out. Ears are internal; external flaps would tear under their own weight.

The heart is not one chambered organ but a chain of thick-walled pumps spaced along the body, each lifting blood only a short vertical distance. In ten g, a tall circulatory column is a death sentence; the keelback never evolved one.

Locomotion is a crawl, not a stride. Six stubby limbs end in broad, padded feet with retractable claws for grip on rock and packed soil. The gait is a slow tripod shuffle. Muscles are short-fibered and enormous relative to the bones they move, arranged so most force is compressive, pressing the body into the ground rather than lifting it. Jumping is impossible. Even rearing onto the hind pairs is a rare, costly display used only in mating contests, and animals that do it too often die of joint failure or aortic rupture.

On this world a stumble from standing height is comparable to a multi-story fall on Earth, so every surface the keelback meets must be met with padding.
